name: C++
description: C++ is a fast and powerful object-oriented programming language.

blocks.html:
Introduction to C++ Programming

What is C++?

C++ is a general-purpose, object-oriented programming language developed by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1979 as an extension of the C programming language. It combines the power of C (procedural programming) with object-oriented programming (OOP) features, making it highly versatile and powerful for building a wide range of applications.

Common applications of C++ include:

  • Operating Systems (e.g., Windows, macOS components)
  • Game Engines (e.g., Unreal Engine)
  • Web Browsers (e.g., Chrome, Firefox)
  • Embedded Systems and IoT devices
  • High-performance software like financial modeling tools

Key Features of C++

  • Object-Oriented Programming: Supports classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.
  • Portability: Write once, run anywhere with little modification.
  • Performance: Close to low-level hardware like C, but with modern features.
  • Standard Template Library (STL): Built-in templates for data structures and algorithms.
  • Multi-Paradigm: Supports procedural, object-oriented, and generic programming.

Basic Structure of a C++ Program

#include <iostream>  // Header file for input and output
using namespace std; // Allows usage of standard names directly

int main() {         // Main function: starting point of execution
    cout << "Hello, World!";  // Print text to the screen
    return 0;        // Indicate successful program termination
}

Understanding C++ Syntax and Its Components

1. Preprocessor Directive

#include <iostream>
The #include directive tells the compiler to include a library before compilation. The <iostream> library enables input and output operations:

  • cout → Output to screen
  • cin → Input from user

2. Namespace Declaration

using namespace std;

This line allows direct access to standard library names like cout and cin. Without it, you'd need to write std::cout every time.

3. Main Function

int main() {
    // Code goes here
    return 0;
}

Every C++ program starts from the main() function.

  • int → The function returns an integer.
  • return 0; → Indicates successful program execution.

4. Statements

cout << "Hello, World!";

The cout object is used to display output to the screen. The << operator inserts data into the output stream.
Every statement must end with a semicolon (;).

5. Comments

// This is a single-line comment

/* 
   This is a 
   multi-line comment 
*/

6. Return Statement

return 0;

Ends the main() function and returns a value to the operating system.
0 means the program ran successfully.

Flow of a C++ Program Execution

  1. Preprocessor Stage: Handles #include and other directives.
  2. Compilation: Converts source code into object code.
  3. Linking: Combines object code with libraries like iostream.
  4. Execution: Runs the final program.

Example: Taking User Input

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int age;
    cout << "Enter your age: ";   // Output message
    cin >> age;                   // Take user input
    cout << "You are " << age << " years old." << endl;
    return 0;
}
New Concepts:
  • cin → Reads input from the user.
  • >> → Extraction operator (opposite of <<).
  • endl → Ends the line and moves output to a new line.

Summary Table

Component Purpose
#include Includes libraries for functions like input/output.
using namespace std; Eliminates the need to write std:: repeatedly.
main() Starting point of program execution.
cout Displays output to the screen.
cin Takes input from the user.
// or /* */ Used to write comments in code.
; (semicolon) Marks the end of a statement.
return 0; Signals successful program execution.

C++ Data Types and Variables

Introduction

In C++, a data type defines the type of data that a variable can store, the amount of memory allocated for it, and the operations that can be performed on it.

Think of data types as containers:

  • A cup for float (decimal numbers)
  • A bottle for int (whole numbers)
  • A jar for string (text)

C++ has three main categories of data types:

  • Primitive (Basic): Core built-in types like int, float, char.
  • Derived: Built using basic data types, e.g., Arrays, Pointers, Functions.
  • User-defined: Created by programmers, e.g., Classes, Structures, Enums.

Primitive Data Types

These are the most commonly used data types in C++:

Data Type Size (Typical) Example Description
int 4 bytes int age = 25; Stores whole numbers
float 4 bytes float pi = 3.14; Stores decimal numbers with ~6-7 digits precision
double 8 bytes double salary = 55000.75; Stores decimal numbers with high precision (~15 digits)
char 1 byte char grade = 'A'; Stores a single character using ASCII values
bool 1 byte bool isStudent = true; Stores true (1) or false (0)

Derived & User-Defined Data Types

Derived Data Types

  • Array: int marks[5] = {90, 85, 88, 92, 79};
  • Pointer: int x = 10; int* ptr = &x
  • Reference: int num = 5; int &ref = num;
  • Function: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

User-Defined Data Types

  • Structure (struct): Groups different data types together 
    struct Student {
    string name;
    int age;
    char grade;
};
  • Class (class): Encapsulates data and functions 
    class Car {
public:
    string brand;
    void start() {
        cout << "Car started!";
    }
};
  • Enumeration (enum): Represents named constants 
    enum Week { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday };

Variables in C++

A variable is a named location in memory used to store data. Its value can change during program execution.

Syntax:

datatype variable_name = value;
Example:
int age = 20;
float pi = 3.14;
char grade = 'A';
bool isStudent = true;

Variable Declaration & Initialization

Type Example
Declaration Only int x;
Initialization Only x = 10;
Declaration + Initialization int x = 10;

Rules for Naming Variables

  • Must start with a letter or underscore (_).
  • Can contain letters, digits, and underscores.
  • Case-sensitive (Age and age are different).
  • Cannot use reserved C++ keywords like int, class, etc.

Live Code Example

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int age = 20;
    float pi = 3.14;
    char grade = 'A';
    bool isStudent = true;
    double salary = 55000.75;

    cout << "Age: " << age << endl;
    cout << "Pi: " << pi << endl;
    cout << "Grade: " << grade << endl;
    cout << "Is Student: " << isStudent << endl;
    cout << "Salary: " << salary << endl;

    return 0;
}

Output:

Age: 20
Pi: 3.14
Grade: A
Is Student: 1
Salary: 55000.75

Checking Memory Size with sizeof

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout << "Size of int: " << sizeof(int) << " bytes" << endl;
    cout << "Size of float: " << sizeof(float) << " bytes" << endl;
    cout << "Size of double: " << sizeof(double) << " bytes" << endl;
    cout << "Size of char: " << sizeof(char) << " byte" << endl;
    cout << "Size of bool: " << sizeof(bool) << " byte" << endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output:

Size of int: 4 bytes
Size of float: 4 bytes
Size of double: 8 bytes
Size of char: 1 byte
Size of bool: 1 byte

Summary

  • Data Types define what kind of data a variable can store.
  • Variables are named memory locations whose values can change during program execution.
  • The sizeof operator helps determine memory usage of data types.
  • Use the correct data type to optimize memory and improve program efficiency.

A for loop is used when the number of iterations is known in advance.

While Loop

Do-While Loop

A do-while loop is similar to a while loop, but it guarantees that the loop body executes at least once.

C++ Arrays

Arrays allow storing multiple values of the same data type under one variable name. They are fundamental for handling lists of data efficiently in C++.

Introduction to Arrays

An array is a collection of variables of the same type stored at contiguous memory locations.
They are useful for:

  • Storing multiple values together
  • Accessing values using an index
  • Efficiently performing operations like search, sort, etc.

1D Arrays

A 1D array is a simple list of elements. Each element can be accessed using its index.

2D Arrays

A 2D array is like a table with rows and columns. It is often used to represent matrices.

Strings in C++

std::string

In C++ you work with text using the std::string class from the <string> header. It grows automatically and comes with many helpful functions. (Older C code used raw char arrays.)

FunctionWhat it does
s.length() / s.size()Number of characters
s[i] / s.at(i)Character at index (at checks the range)
s.substr(pos, len)Part of the string
s.find("x")Index of first match, or string::npos if not found
s.replace(pos, len, "new")Replace part of the string
s.append("x") / s + tJoin strings
s == t, s < tCompare strings

A string is a sequence of characters, so you can loop through it with a range-based for. Use char &ch (a reference) when you want to change the characters.

  • stoi() / stod() turn text into numbers.

C++ Functions

Functions help organize code into smaller reusable blocks. Click Run demo to see output.

Introduction to Functions

Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform specific tasks. They improve readability, reusability, and maintainability.

Pass by Value

A copy of the variable is passed to the function. Changes do not affect the original variable.

Pass by Reference

The actual variable memory address is passed. Changes inside the function affect the original variable.

Function Overloading

Functions can have the same name but different parameter types.

Recursive Function

A recursive function calls itself until a base condition is met.

Summary of Functions

Functions make code modular, reusable, and easy to maintain.

C++ Pointers

A pointer in C++ is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. They are essential for dynamic memory allocation, working with arrays, and passing data efficiently to functions.

Introduction to Pointers

Pointers allow direct access to memory addresses, making programs more flexible and powerful.
Key concepts:

  • Pointers store addresses instead of actual values.
  • The & operator is used to get the address of a variable.
  • The * operator (dereference) is used to access the value at that address.

Declaring and Using Pointers

To declare a pointer, use the * symbol:

  • int *ptr; → A pointer to an integer.
  • char *cptr; → A pointer to a character.

Pointer Arithmetic

Pointers can be incremented or decremented to move between memory locations. This is especially useful when working with arrays.

Pointer to Pointer (Double Pointer)

A pointer to a pointer is a variable that stores the address of another pointer. It is often used in dynamic memory and multidimensional arrays.

topics.title: Static & Dynamic Memory

blocks.html:
Static & Dynamic Memory Management in C++

Learn how memory is allocated and managed at compile-time and runtime in C++.

What is Memory Management?

Memory management determines how variables and data structures are stored and managed during program execution. C++ provides both static memory allocation (at compile time) and dynamic memory allocation (at runtime).

Static Memory Allocation

Memory is allocated at compile time. The size and lifetime of variables are fixed throughout the program.
  • Fast and efficient
  • Less flexible (size cannot change)
  • Memory is automatically freed when the function ends

Dynamic Memory Allocation

Memory is allocated at runtime using new and manually released using delete.
  • Flexible: Memory can be allocated based on user input
  • Efficient for large or unknown data sizes
  • Programmer is responsible for freeing memory

Dynamic Array

Create an array dynamically based on user input size using new[] and free it using delete[].

Dynamic 2D Array

Allocate memory for a two-dimensional array at runtime.

Memory Leak Example

A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory is not freed, causing wasted memory. 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void createLeak() {
    int *ptr = new int(100); // Memory allocated but not freed
}

int main() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        createLeak(); // Memory keeps leaking
    }
    cout << "Memory leak occurred!";
    return 0;
}
❗ **Solution:** Always use delete or smart pointers like unique_ptr or shared_ptr.

Using Smart Pointers

Smart pointers automatically manage memory and prevent leaks.

Structures & Enums

struct: Your Own Data Type

A structure groups variables of different types under one name. It is perfect for records, like a student with a name, age and GPA. Members are accessed with the dot operator (.).

• A struct is almost the same as a class: the only difference is that its members are public by default (in a class they are private).
  • Pass structs to functions by const reference (const Student &s) to avoid copying.

enum: Named Constants

An enumeration gives readable names to a small set of fixed values. Prefer enum class: its names stay inside the enum (Level::Beginner) and it does not silently convert to int.

topics.title: Class & Object

blocks.html:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in C++

A complete guide to understanding OOP concepts, classes, objects, constructors, destructors, and more with examples.

OOP in one shot

What is OOP?

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm that models real-world entities using classes and objects. It helps to build modular, reusable, and maintainable code.

Four Pillars of OOP:

  • Encapsulation: Binding data and functions into one unit (class).
  • Abstraction: Hiding unnecessary implementation details.
  • Inheritance: Reusing properties and behaviors from an existing class.
  • Polymorphism: Functions or methods behaving differently based on context.

Example from real life: A Car has properties like brand, speed, and actions like drive and brake. This matches exactly how a class works in C++.

Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint that defines properties (data members) and actions (methods). An object is a real instance of a class.

blocks.output:
Brand: BMW
Speed: 200 km/h
Brand: Audi
Speed: 220 km/h

blocks.html:
Access Specifiers

Access specifiers define how class members are accessed from outside the class.

  • public: Accessible from anywhere.
  • private: Accessible only inside the class.
  • protected: Accessible in the class and its derived classes.

Constructors

A constructor is a special method that automatically runs when an object is created. It is used to initialize data members.

Destructors

A destructor is automatically called when an object goes out of scope. It is used for cleanup, like releasing memory or closing files.

Nested Classes

C++ allows a class to be defined inside another class. This is useful for grouping related classes together.

Polymorphism (Method Overriding)

Polymorphism allows methods to have the same name but behave differently in different contexts.

Encapsulation & Abstraction in C++

Understand the differences between Encapsulation and Abstraction with detailed examples and explanations.

Introduction

Encapsulation and Abstraction are two fundamental pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). They both deal with **hiding data and complexity**, but they are not the same thing.

  • Encapsulation: Bundling data and methods together in a class and controlling access using access specifiers like private, public, and protected.
  • Abstraction: Hiding implementation details and exposing only essential features to the user.

Encapsulation in C++

**Encapsulation** is like a protective shield that prevents direct access to data members. Instead of directly modifying the data, we use methods like getters and setters.

Real-life example: A bank account system hides the balance from direct access and provides deposit/withdraw functions to interact with it.

Abstraction in C++

**Abstraction** focuses on hiding **implementation details** while only showing what is necessary to the user.

Real-life example: When you use an ATM, you don't know how it internally processes your request. You only see options like "Withdraw", "Deposit", and "Check Balance".

Encapsulation vs Abstraction

Encapsulation Abstraction
Wraps data and functions into one unit. Shows only essential details to the user.
Achieved using classes and access specifiers. Achieved using abstract classes and interfaces.
Focuses on data hiding and protection. Focuses on hiding complexity.
Example: Private bank balance with deposit/withdraw methods. Example: ATM operations shown without implementation details.

C++ Inheritance & Types

Learn about inheritance in C++, why it is important, and explore different types with real-life examples and outputs.

What is Inheritance?

Inheritance is an important feature of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). It allows a derived class (child) to acquire properties and behaviors from a base class (parent).

It helps in:

  • Code Reusability – Write common code once and reuse it.
  • Better Maintainability – Easy to maintain and update.
  • Logical Structure – Represents real-world relationships like Car is a Vehicle.

Types of Inheritance

There are five main types of inheritance in C++:

  • Single Inheritance
  • Multiple Inheritance
  • Multilevel Inheritance
  • Hierarchical Inheritance
  • Hybrid Inheritance

1. Single Inheritance

A derived class inherits from a single base class. Example: A Car inherits features from a Vehicle.

2. Multiple Inheritance

A derived class inherits from more than one base class.

Example: A FlyingCar inherits from both Car and Airplane.

blocks.output:
Driving on road
Flying in the air
Transforming between car and airplane mode

blocks.html:
3. Multilevel Inheritance

A derived class inherits from another derived class, forming a chain-like hierarchy. Example: SportsCar → Car → Vehicle

blocks.output:
Vehicle started
Car horn!
Turbo Boost Activated!

blocks.html:
4. Hierarchical Inheritance

In this type, multiple derived classes inherit from the same base class. Example: Both Car and Bike inherit from Vehicle.

blocks.output:
Vehicle started
Car is driving
Vehicle started
Bike is riding

blocks.html:
5. Hybrid Inheritance

A combination of two or more inheritance types. It may cause the Diamond Problem, which can be solved using virtual inheritance.

Summary Table

Type Description Example
Single One derived class from one base class. Car → Vehicle
Multiple One derived class from multiple base classes. FlyingCar → Car + Airplane
Multilevel Chain-like inheritance relationship. SportsCar → Car → Vehicle
Hierarchical Multiple derived classes from one base class. Car, Bike → Vehicle
Hybrid Combination of two or more inheritance types. Diamond structure example

Polymorphism in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

Learn how polymorphism allows objects of different classes to be treated as a common type, making your C++ programs more flexible and maintainable.

Introduction to Polymorphism

Polymorphism is one of the fundamental concepts in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). The term polymorphism comes from Greek, meaning "many forms". It allows a single interface to represent different underlying data types or classes.

For example, a function named draw() may draw different shapes like Circle or Rectangle depending on which object calls it.

Types of Polymorphism

Polymorphism is mainly classified into two types:

  1. Compile-time Polymorphism (Static Polymorphism)
  2. Run-time Polymorphism (Dynamic Polymorphism)

1. Compile-time Polymorphism

Resolved during compilation. Achieved through:

  • Method Overloading
  • Operator Overloading

Method Overloading

Multiple methods with the same name but different parameters. The compiler chooses which method to call based on arguments.

Operator Overloading

Operator overloading allows redefining operators for custom behavior. Example: Adding two complex numbers with the + operator.

2. Run-time Polymorphism

Resolved at runtime using virtual functions and function overriding.

Example: Virtual Functions

Summary Table

Type How Achieved When Resolved Example
Compile-time Polymorphism Method Overloading, Operator Overloading Compile-time add(int a, int b), add(double a, double b)
Run-time Polymorphism Method Overriding, Virtual Functions Run-time Derived class overrides base class method

Conclusion

Polymorphism is a cornerstone of OOP, allowing for flexible and scalable code design. By leveraging polymorphism, developers can build systems that are easier to extend and maintain.

Operator Overloading

Teach Operators About Your Classes

Operators like +, == and << already work for numbers and strings. With operator overloading you tell C++ what they mean for your own classes, so a + b reads naturally. An overloaded operator is just a function named operator+, operator==, and so on.

• Operators that read or compare an object should be const (... const).
  • operator<< must be a normal (often friend) function because the left side is cout, not your object.

Prefix and Postfix ++

Both ++c and c++ use the same operator name. C++ tells them apart with a dummy int parameter for the postfix version.

Rules to Remember

  • You cannot overload: ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof.
  • You cannot invent new operators or change precedence.
  • At least one operand must be a user-defined type.
  • Keep the meaning natural: do not make + subtract!

Friend Function & Friend Class in C++

In C++, friend functions and friend classes allow selective access to private and protected members of a class, enabling controlled flexibility while maintaining encapsulation.

Friend Function

A friend function is a non-member function that can access the private and protected members of a class. It is declared inside the class using the friend keyword.

Key Points:

  • It is not a member of the class.
  • It has access to private and protected members.
  • Friendship is one-way: the function can access the class members, but the class cannot access the function’s private members.
  • Overuse can break encapsulation, so use only when necessary.

Example:

Friend Class

A friend class allows all member functions of another class to access its private and protected members.

Key Points:

  • All methods of the friend class can access private/protected members of the original class.
  • Friendship is one-way; the original class members are accessible to the friend class, but not vice versa.
  • Used when two classes are closely related and need mutual access to private data.

Example:

Rules and Important Notes

  • Friendship is not inherited: if class B is a friend of class A, derived classes of B are not automatically friends of A.
  • Friend functions can be standalone functions or member functions of another class.
  • Friend classes and functions cannot be called with dot operator like normal member functions unless they are member functions of another class.
  • Use friendship to enable controlled access between related classes, without breaking encapsulation everywhere.

When to Use

  • Two or more classes are tightly coupled and need access to each other’s private data.
  • Helper functions that require access to class internals without being part of the class.
  • Overloading operators that need access to private members.
  • Implementing controlled access to internal members for performance or design purposes.

Templates

Write Once, Use With Any Type

Without templates you would write maxOfInt, maxOfDouble, maxOfString... one copy per type. A template is a blueprint: the compiler creates the real function for each type you use. T is a placeholder for "some type".

• The compiler usually deduces T from the arguments (maxOf(3, 9)).
  • Or you can say it yourself: maxOf<string>(...).
  • Both arguments must give the same T: maxOf(3, 2.5) will not compile.

Class Templates

Classes can be templates too. This is how vector<int> and map<string, int> are built. With classes you always write the type in angle brackets.

Remember

  • Template code normally lives completely in header files.
  • The type must support the operations used inside (maxOf needs >).
  • Use typename or class in the angle brackets, they mean the same.
  • Templates are the foundation of the STL, the next lesson.

Exception Handling

try, throw, catch

An exception is C++'s way of reporting that something went wrong without crashing the program. Put risky code in a try block, signal a problem with throw, and deal with it in a catch block. When an exception is thrown, C++ jumps straight to the matching catch and skips the rest of the try block.

blocks.output:
10 / 2 = 5
Now trying 10 / 0...
Error: Cannot divide by zero
Program continues normally

blocks.html:
• Catch by const reference (const exception &e) to avoid copying.
  • e.what() returns the message.

Your Own Exception Types

Inherit from a standard exception class (like runtime_error) to make errors that describe your program. You can have several catch blocks; the first one that matches is used, so put specific types before general ones.

blocks.output:
Withdrew 30, balance 70
Bad input: Amount must be positive
Insufficient funds: need 430.000000 more

blocks.html:
Standard Exceptions

Class (in )Typical meaning
invalid_argumentA function got a bad value
out_of_rangeIndex outside the valid range (e.g. vector::at)
runtime_errorSomething failed while running
logic_errorA mistake in the program logic
bad_allocnew could not get memory

Use catch (...) as a last resort to catch anything.

Good Habits

  • Use exceptions for unexpected problems, not for normal flow like "user pressed no".
  • Never throw from a destructor.
  • Clean up resources with smart pointers (RAII), so nothing leaks when an exception skips code.

STL Basics: vector, map & Algorithms

What is the STL?

The Standard Template Library is a set of ready-made, well-tested tools built with templates: containers (store data), algorithms (work on data) and iterators (connect the two). Before writing your own array or sort, check the STL first.

ContainerHeaderThink of it as
vector<T><vector>A resizable array
map<K, V><map>A dictionary of key to value, sorted by key
set<T><set>A sorted collection with no duplicates
queue<T> / stack<T><queue> / <stack>First-in-first-out / last-in-first-out

vector and Algorithms

A vector is the container you will use most. Algorithms from <algorithm> take a range: v.begin() to v.end().

Sorted: 60 72 79 88 95
Highest: 95
60 is present
Count of 88: 1

map and set

map stores pairs and keeps them sorted by key. set stores unique values. Both find items quickly.

File Handling

Files in C++

Programs lose their variables when they end. Files let you keep data permanently. Include <fstream> and use:

ClassPurpose
ofstreamOutput file stream: write to a file
ifstreamInput file stream: read from a file
fstreamBoth reading and writing

Streams work just like cout and cin: you use << to write and >> or getline to read.

The file notes.txt appears in the same folder where the program runs.

Append Mode and Checking for Errors

Opening an ofstream normally erases the file. Add ios::app to add to the end instead. Always check that the file opened (is_open() or if (!stream)), because the file might not exist or you might not have permission.

blocks.output:
Words in file: 5
Missing file detected

blocks.html:
Open Modes

ModeMeaning
ios::inOpen for reading
ios::outOpen for writing (erases existing content)
ios::appAppend to the end
ios::binaryBinary file instead of text

Combine modes with |, for example ios::out | ios::app.

Good Habits

  • Close files when done (close()), or let them close automatically when the stream goes out of scope.
  • Check every open: never assume the file exists.
  • Use while (getline(in, line)) to read all lines. Do not loop on eof().
